512.title: Six of Shawwal
512.hook: six fasts after Ramadan are like fasting the year (Muslim)
512.howItsDone: Many Muslims fast six voluntary days in Shawwal, the month after Ramadan, starting after the day of Eid; some fast them consecutively and others spread them through the month.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the takbirat of Eid morning, and your line, allahu akbar on the way.

The morning after Eid, the house looks like a party happened: plates in the sink, sweets nobody can face, new clothes hung back up. For a month the whole rhythm of life was different: the pre-dawn meal, the long afternoon, the date at sunset, the night prayer. Now, suddenly, lunch is back. For some there's relief. For some, a strange little grief, as if a guest left without saying goodbye. The month after Ramadan is called Shawwal, and tucked into it is a quiet custom: not one more month of fasting, just six more days.

The custom rests on a hadith. In Sahih Muslim, the companion Abu Ayyub al-Ansari reports that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said whoever fasts Ramadan and then follows it with six days of Shawwal, it is as if they had fasted the whole span of time. Another report, from the companion Thawban, gives the arithmetic. A good deed is counted ten times over, a principle the Qur'an itself states. So thirty days of Ramadan count as three hundred, and six more count as sixty. Three hundred and sixty: roughly a year, folded into five weeks. A few practical things. You don't fast on the day of Eid itself; the Prophet forbade fasting on the two Eids. After that, the six can be kept back to back, right after Eid, or spread through the month, a Monday here, a Thursday there; scholars have discussed both, and many say either is fine. People who missed days of Ramadan, through illness, travel, or for women, their monthly period, often ask which comes first, the make-up days or the six. Here the schools give different answers, and many people simply ask a scholar they trust. Not everyone in early Islam was enthusiastic. Imam Malik, the scholar of Medina, is reported to have disliked making it a fixed custom, worried people might start treating it as part of Ramadan. Other schools recommend it. For those who keep them, the six keep the door from slamming shut. Ramadan ends, but the habit doesn't vanish overnight; a small part of it stays in the week.
screen: `A HADITH IN SAHIH MUSLIM.` · `THIRTY TIMES TEN, PLUS SIX TIMES TEN.` · `NOT ON EID; TOGETHER OR SPREAD OUT.` · `KEEP THE DOOR FROM SLAMMING SHUT.`

segments.voice: Picture next week and find one calm day, no big dinner, no hard workout. If you're able, and it's safe for your health, decide to fast it from dawn to sunset; if fasting isn't possible for you, plan to eat one meal that day slowly, with no screen, the way a fast is broken at sunset. If you pray, you can make your intention quietly now.

513.title: The ten days
513.hook: no days are dearer to Allah for good deeds than the first ten of Dhul Hijjah (Bukhari)
513.howItsDone: In the first ten days of Dhul Hijjah many Muslims increase prayer, charity, remembrance and takbir; many fast the day of 'Arafah, and some fast the first nine days.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shawwal, and six more fasts after the month ends. Your line was six more.

Ramadan is usually the month that comes to mind first when the holiest days of the Islamic year come up, and its nights carry Laylat al-Qadr. But a hadith in Bukhari points somewhere else. It names a different stretch of days, about two months after Ramadan ends, at the start of the last month of the year, the month of pilgrimage. While pilgrims are heading for Mecca, everyone else, at home, is also in a season. Today: the ten days.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn 'Abbas reports that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said there are no days in which good deeds are more beloved to God than these, meaning the first ten days of Dhul Hijjah. The companions were startled. Not even striving in the path of God? Not even that, he said, except a man who goes out with his life and his wealth and comes back with nothing. An ordinary good deed, done in these ten days, is set beside the hardest sacrifice there is. Commentators also connect the days to the Qur'an. Surah Al-Fajr opens with an oath, by the dawn, and ten nights, and commentators going back to Ibn 'Abbas understood those ten nights as these. And Surah Al-Hajj speaks of remembering God's name on appointed days, which Ibn 'Abbas is reported to have explained as the ten. What do people do? More of what they already do: extra prayer, charity, reading, kindness. Some fast the first nine days. Others fast at least the ninth, the day of 'Arafah, when the pilgrims stand on the plain; a hadith in Sahih Muslim hopes that fast wipes away the faults of the year before and the year after. Some companions, Bukhari notes, used to walk through the markets in these days saying the takbir aloud, and people around them took it up. And a hadith in Muslim says that someone planning to offer a sacrifice for Eid shouldn't cut their hair or nails from the start of the month, a small mark in the body that the season has begun. The point isn't a new set of rules. It's a window: the same deeds, in a season when they weigh more.

Picture doing it near the end, when you're tired; if it still fits, keep it. If you pray, you can make your intention now.

514.title: Eid al-Adha: days of tashriq
514.hook: takbir after prayers for the days after Eid
514.howItsDone: On Eid al-Adha Muslims who are able offer an animal sacrifice and share the meat with family, neighbors and people in need; many say the takbir after the daily prayers through the days of tashriq, the eleventh to thirteenth of Dhul Hijjah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first ten days of Dhul Hijjah, and your line, the best ten days.

In a lot of Muslim homes, the morning of Eid al-Adha has a particular sound. Not just greetings and children, but bags: plastic bags of meat divided on the kitchen counter, knotted, labeled, carried next door, driven across town, handed to the man who sweeps the street. Phones buzzing with addresses. Someone always asking whether the neighbors on the third floor got theirs. It's the feast of the sacrifice, and it doesn't end in one day.
screen: `A FEAST THAT DOESN'T END IN A DAY.`

segments.voice: Eid al-Adha falls on the tenth of Dhul Hijjah, the day after the pilgrims stand at 'Arafah. It remembers Ibrahim, who in Surah As-Saffat saw in a dream that he was to sacrifice his son, and both of them submitted, and God ransomed the son with a tremendous sacrifice. Muslims who are able offer an animal, a sheep, a goat, a share in a cow or camel, and the Qur'an tells them in Surah Al-Hajj to eat of it and to feed the one who is content and the one who asks. Many divide it in thirds: for the household, for friends and neighbors, and for those in need, a custom scholars recommend rather than require. The same surah adds a line often quoted at Eid: neither the flesh nor the blood reaches God; what reaches Him is your devotion, your taqwa. Then come three more days, the eleventh, twelfth and thirteenth, called the days of tashriq. A hadith in Sahih Muslim describes them in a phrase that became today's line: they are days of eating and drinking, and of remembering God. Fasting is not allowed on them. And the remembrance has a shape. Surah Al-Baqarah says to remember God through the numbered days, and many Muslims say the takbir after each of the five daily prayers, from the dawn of 'Arafah until the afternoon of the thirteenth. It begins: God is greatest, God is greatest, there is no god but God. The schools differ a little on the exact start and end. A feast, a share for the neighbor, and a refrain after every prayer, across the four days of the feast.
screen: `THE TENTH: IBRAHIM'S RANSOM.` · `EAT, AND FEED THE ONE WHO ASKS.` · `NOT THE FLESH: THE DEVOTION.` · `THREE DAYS OF TASHRIQ.`

segments.voice: Picture the people who live closest to you: the door across the hall, the house over the fence, the colleague at the next desk. Pick one, maybe someone you've never really spoken to, and think what you could bring them; it needn't be meat or anything grand, just a plate of something you cooked or a box of fruit. If you pray, you can say God is greatest, quietly, as you picture handing it over.

515.title: A moving calendar
515.hook: a lunar year is about eleven days shorter, so Ramadan visits every season over thirty-three years
515.tomorrow: Who feeds me and heals me
515.howItsDone: Muslims date Ramadan, Hajj and the other holy days by the lunar Hijri calendar, beginning months by sighting or calculating the new crescent, so the festivals move about eleven days earlier each solar year.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Eid al-Adha and the days of tashriq, and your line, eat, drink, remember. Today, the last of the holy days.

Two cousins, years apart in age, can remember childhood Ramadans in different seasons. One remembers long summer days, the fast running late into the evening, playing outside in the heat with a dry mouth. The other remembers short winter fasts, breaking it before the early dark, homework at the table afterward. Same month, same rules, a completely different experience. That's not a change in the religion. It's the calendar, doing exactly what it was built to do.

The Hijri calendar follows the moon. Each month begins when the new crescent, the hilal, is seen or reckoned. Twelve lunar months add up to about three hundred fifty-four days, roughly eleven days shorter than the solar year. So every year Ramadan arrives about eleven days earlier by the solar calendar, and over roughly thirty-three years it slides backward through every season and comes round again. The Qur'an names this rhythm. In Surah Al-Baqarah people ask about the new moons, and the answer is that they are markers of time for people and for the pilgrimage. Surah At-Tawbah says the number of months with God is twelve, and criticizes the practice called nasi', postponing a month; some historians understand that as an older Arabian habit of adding a month so the year kept step with the seasons, while others read it as shifting a sacred month. The Qur'anic calendar lets the months move. Here's what that does. Nobody's Ramadan is always the hard one, or always the easy one. Over a lifetime, someone in the far north gets long summer fasts and short winter ones, and when the north has its long fasts, the south has its short ones. Hajj travels through the seasons too. And the moon is something anyone can see, from a roof or a field, without a printed calendar. These two weeks of holy days move with it: the Hijri new year, 'Ashura's two memories, Mawlid, the night journey, Sha'ban's getting ready, Ramadan's book and seclusion and khatm, the takbir of Eid, six more, the ten days, and the feast of the sacrifice. Every one of them drifts through the seasons, together. Tomorrow, back to the book, and the middle of the Qur'an.
screen: `TWELVE MONTHS BY THE MOON.` · `ELEVEN DAYS EARLIER EACH YEAR.` · `EVERY SEASON IN THIRTY-THREE YEARS.` · `THE HOLY DAYS MOVE TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Look out the window, or picture it: what season is it where you are, and is it a season of long days or short ones? Then let your mind run thirty-three years forward, when the same month will have visited every one of those seasons. If you pray, you can hold that thought as a quiet hope.

516.title: Who feeds me and heals me
516.hook: Ibrahim describes his Lord: who created me, guides me, feeds me, and heals me when I'm ill (26:78–80)
516.carry: he feeds me; he heals me
516.howItsDone: Many Muslims say bismillah before eating and alhamdulillah after, and pray for the sick with words from the Prophet's practice that name God as the Healer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hilal, the new moon that moves the holy days through every season. Your line was ramadan visits every season. Today, a new block begins.

Back to the book, and to its middle. This block opens with Surah Ash-Shu'ara, the Poets, the twenty-sixth. Ash-Shu'ara is long and full of prophets: Musa, Ibrahim, Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut, Shu'ayb. After each story comes the same refrain: in this is a sign, and your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful. Today's verses come from Ibrahim's story. He asks his father and his people what they worship. Idols, they say, and their fathers did the same. And Ibrahim answers by describing, simply, the One he worships.
screen: `BLOCK C: THE MIDDLE OF THE BOOK.`
`A SURAH OF PROPHETS AND A REFRAIN.`

segments.voice: Ibrahim's answer is made of verbs, and in Arabic nearly every one ends in the sound for me: created me, guides me, feeds me, heals me. Pickthall: "Who created me, and He doth guide me, And Who feedeth me and watereth me. And when I sicken, then He healeth me." He goes on: who causes me to die and then gives me life, and who, he hopes, will forgive his faults on the Day of Judgment. Look at what he picks: not the stars or the mountains, but the things a person lives through every day. Being made. Being shown the way. Breakfast. A glass of water. A fever that breaks. It's a whole theology at the level of the kitchen table. Then a small detail in the grammar. Every line says He did it: He created, He guides, He feeds, He gives drink. Until the illness. There Ibrahim doesn't say, when He makes me sick. He says, when I sicken. Many commentators read that as adab, courtesy: he speaks of God in connection with the good, and takes the hard thing onto himself. Not as a theory of where illness comes from, but as a way of speaking. The healing goes straight back to God. The same shape runs through how many Muslims pray for the sick: the illness named plainly, the healing asked of God. A hadith in Bukhari records the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, visiting the sick, asking God, the Healer, to heal, with a healing that leaves no illness behind. The words are short, but they cover a life: made, guided, fed, given drink, healed, and in the end, he hopes, forgiven.
screen: `MADE, GUIDED, FED, GIVEN DRINK.` · `A THEOLOGY OF THE KITCHEN TABLE.` · `WHEN I SICKEN: A COURTESY.` · `THEN HE HEALS ME.`

517.title: A sound heart
517.hook: the Day when wealth and sons won't help, only one who comes with a sound heart (26:88–89)
517.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite Ibrahim's prayer from Ash-Shu'ara and ask God for a sound heart, and some make a habit of forgiving others before sleeping.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shifa', healing, in Ibrahim's list of what his Lord does. Your line was he feeds me; he heals me.

Airports have a rule about what you can carry on. A small bag, a weight limit, and a whole list of things that have to be left behind at the gate. People stand at the security tray deciding, fast, what matters. Ibrahim's prayer in Ash-Shu'ara keeps going after yesterday's verses, and it ends at a kind of gate. A day when almost everything people spend their lives collecting has to be left on the other side. There's only one thing he says gets through.

Ibrahim asks for wisdom, for good company, for an honest name among those who come later, for forgiveness for his father. Then he asks not to be disgraced on the day people are raised, and describes that day. Pickthall: "The day when wealth and sons avail not (any man) Save him who bringeth unto Allah a whole heart." Pickthall says a whole heart. The Arabic is qalb salim. Qalb is heart. Salim means sound, safe, intact, unbroken. So what makes a heart salim? Commentators gave several answers, and they stack. Free of associating anything with God. Free of doubt. And some added: free of malice, envy and grudges toward other people. The Qur'an uses the same phrase once more, in As-Saffat, of Ibrahim himself: he came to his Lord with a sound heart. So the one who names the sound heart is the one the Qur'an elsewhere says had it. There's a hadith in both Bukhari and Muslim that sits right beside this verse. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said that in the body there is a lump of flesh; when it is sound, the whole body is sound, and when it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt, and it is the heart. Elsewhere the Qur'an calls wealth and children an adornment of this life. They just don't come through the gate. What comes through is a heart, and whether it arrives in one piece.

If you pray, you can ask for a sound heart, and for good for that person.
Qalb salim. A sound heart, whole and safe, free of shirk, doubt and grudge: the one thing Ibrahim says avails on the Day. Today's word.
Your line: bring a sound heart. Everything else gets left behind at the tray. Until tomorrow.

518.title: Lower your wing
518.hook: lower your wing to the believers who follow you (26:215)
518.howItsDone: Muslims read 26:215 alongside the Prophet's example of humility with his companions, and many quote the parallel verse in Al-Isra about lowering the wing of humility to one's parents.

segments.voice: Yesterday: qalb salim, the sound heart Ibrahim says gets through. Your line was bring a sound heart.

Watch a hen when the sky darkens. She doesn't make a speech. She crouches, spreads her wings low, and the chicks run under. A big bird coming in to land drops low, slows down, and comes close to the ground. A raised wing is for flying, for display, for looking big. A lowered wing is for landing, and for covering someone. Near the end of Ash-Shu'ara, after all the prophets' stories, the surah turns to the Prophet himself, and gives him that picture.

The verses come in a row. First: warn your nearest kin. Bukhari reports that after this the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ climbed the hill of Safa in Mecca and called the clans of Quraysh by name. Then, right after the warning, comes tenderness. Pickthall: "And lower thy wing (in kindness) unto those believers who follow thee." Pickthall adds in kindness in brackets, because the Arabic picture, khafd al-janah, lowering the wing, already means it: gentleness, humility, coming down to someone's level. Notice who it's addressed to. The leader. The one everybody follows. It's not, follow humbly. It's, lead humbly. The Qur'an uses the same image for children and parents in Al-Isra: lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy. There the young lower the wing to the old. Here the one in charge lowers it to those who look up to him. Either way, the person with the power to fly over others is told to come down and cover them. And the reports of his life keep small examples: mending his own sandal, helping in his household, and telling a woman who wanted a word with him to choose any street, and he would sit with her there. This week was a slow landing after the holy days. Six more fasts. The best ten days. Eat, drink, remember. A calendar that moves through every season. Then back to the book: he feeds me, he heals me; bring a sound heart. And today, lower the wing.
screen: `FIRST: WARN YOUR NEAREST KIN.` · `KHAFD AL-JANAH: LOWER THE WING.` · `NOT FOLLOW HUMBLY: LEAD HUMBLY.` · `PARENTS, AND THOSE WHO FOLLOW.`
